title: Diop's Header. Bounou's Save. Morocco Stun the Netherlands in a Monterrey Shootout.
excerpt: A 91st-minute equaliser and a penalty-shootout masterclass send Morocco past the Dutch and into a Round of 16 date with Canada in Houston — continuing the Atlas Lions' transformation into a genuine World Cup force.
body:
For 89 minutes, it looked like Morocco's World Cup was over.

Cody Gakpo had scored the kind of goal that feels like the last word — a composed finish from close range in the 72nd minute, conjured from a spinning pass by Crysencio Summerville that sliced through Morocco's backline at Estadio Monterrey. The Netherlands, a team built to absorb pressure and strike on the counter, appeared to have found the formula.

Then Issa Diop happened.

The Fulham centre-back, who only switched his international allegiance from France to Morocco earlier this year, rose to meet Chemsdine Talbi's long cross in the 91st minute and buried a header past Bart Verbruggen. It was his first international goal. It came in the most consequential moment of his career. And it sent the Moroccan end of the stadium — a wall of red stretching across the Monterrey stands — into delirium.

## A Penalty Shootout for the Ages


![World Cup — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/fb/Kitzbuehel_slalom_ganslernhang_2010.jpg)


What followed was a penalty shootout so chaotic it defied belief.

Teun Koopmeiners, the Dutch midfielder, went first and squeezed his shot inside the post. Morocco blinked when Neil El Aynaoui clattered the crossbar. Then Justin Kluivert clipped the outside of the opposite post. Soufiane Rahimi's attempt was partially saved by Verbruggen — but the ball squirmed under the goalkeeper and was nudged over the line by his own heel, restoring parity at 1-1.



> **"## What Comes Next

Morocco now travel to Houston to face Canada in the Round of 16 on July 4 — a fixture that will draw massive crowds from both communities across North America."**


Wout Weghorst rocketed his penalty past Bounou. Sunderland's Talbi — already the architect of the equaliser — coolly beat Verbruggen to make it 2-2. Quinten Timber then yanked his shot wide. Achraf Hakimi smashed the post. Three Dutch misses, two Moroccan ones, and a ball that arguably should have been saved but wasn't.

At 2-2 after four rounds, Summerville — the man whose assist had given the Netherlands the lead — stepped up. Bounou read the shot perfectly, diving left to parry it with his outstretched hand. Ismael Saibari stepped up and buried the winner. Morocco advanced 3-2 on penalties.


## Morocco's Quiet Revolution


![Crysencio Summerville — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/15/Crysencio_Summerville_of_West_Ham_United.jpeg)


This is no longer the same Morocco that surprised everyone at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar by reaching the semi-finals. That run was powered by emotion and defensive organisation. This team is deeper, more controlled, and arguably more dangerous.

Walid Regragui's side dominated possession for long stretches in Monterrey, fashioning the better chances before the break. Verbruggen produced a series of outstanding saves to deny Ayoub Bouaddi's close-range header and El Aynaoui's powerful effort in the first half alone. Hakimi rattled the crossbar before the Dutch had even found their rhythm. Morocco took 11 shots across 120 minutes — the Netherlands managed just six.

Diop's story is emblematic of the broader project. Born in Toulouse to a Senegalese-Malian father, he played for France's youth teams before switching to Morocco. He is one of several European-born players of North African descent who have chosen to represent the Atlas Lions, a diaspora talent pipeline that mirrors what India's own sports policy debates have been circling around for years.

## The Dutch Curse Deepens

For the Netherlands, this was a familiar kind of agony. It was their third consecutive World Cup exit on penalties — following shootout losses to Argentina in both 2014 and 2022. Ronald Koeman's side, ranked seventh in the world, never imposed itself on the match. The Dutch were tentative, atypically defensive, and seemed to be playing for a shootout even before one arrived.


![Chemsdine Talbi — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f1/Chemsdine_Talbi_Brazil_V_Morocco_13_June_2026-203.jpg)


"The team that had the better of play for almost the entire game advanced," Fox Sports' match analysis noted. "Morocco was the more aggressive team and came to play."

The three-time World Cup finalists — still the best team never to win the tournament — head home having played just four matches in this edition.

## What Comes Next

Morocco now travel to Houston to face Canada in the Round of 16 on July 4 — a fixture that will draw massive crowds from both communities across North America. Canada, co-hosting the tournament, advanced past South Africa 1-0 in their Round of 32 opener.

For the Indian diaspora watching this World Cup unfold across living rooms and fan zones in Houston, New York, and Los Angeles, the penalty drama in Monterrey was yet another reminder of why this tournament — being staged on home soil for the first time in over three decades — has felt different. The next wave of knockout matches arrives on Tuesday, with France facing Sweden in East Rutherford and Ivory Coast meeting Norway in Arlington, before the tournament descends on the Bay Area on Wednesday: USA vs Bosnia and Herzegovina at Levi's Stadium in Santa Clara.

The group stage is done. The World Cup has found its gear.

*Sources: Reuters, NBC Sports, Fox Sports, Field Level Media*
